claim: Svep1 is required for facial collecting lymphatic vessel formation in a Vegfc-independent manner.
source: Svep1 is required for facial collecting lymphatic vessel formation in a Vegfc-independent manner
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing svep1 mutants specifically lack the FCLV while retaining other facial lymphatic structures, and that vegfc/ccbe1/adamts mutants show the opposite pattern (Figure 1).

claim: svep1 mutants show a specific loss of the facial collecting lymphatic vessel (FCLV) at 5 dpf.
source: svep1 mutants showed a specific loss of the FCLV
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal imaging showing absence of FCLV in svep1 mutants (Figure 1A).

claim: Mutants for Vegfc/Vegfr3 pathway members (ccbe1, adamts3/14, and vegfc) retain the facial collecting lymphatic vessel (FCLV) but lack all other structures of the facial lymphatics.
source: While mutants for Vegfc/Vegfr3 pathway members like ccbe1, adamts3/14, and vegfc retained the facial collecting lymphatic vessel (FCLV) (red dotted line in Figure 1A, B) but lacked all other structures of the facial lymphatics
evidence: Shown by confocal imaging of facial lymphatics in these mutants (Figure 1B).

claim: svep1 is expressed in cells juxtaposed to the sprouting LECs around the PHS at 50 hpf.
source: We detected svep1 expression in cells juxtaposed to the sprouting LECs around the PHS, which later will form the FCLV
evidence: Demonstrated using transgenic reporter lines showing svep1 expression pattern (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).

claim: vegfc expression at 50 hpf is more restricted to the lateral facial lymphatic sprout arising from the CCV.
source: while vegfc expression was more restricted to the lateral facial lymphatic sprout arising from the CCV in all embryos analyzed (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Shown by transgenic reporter line imaging (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).

claim: Simultaneous interference of both Vegfc and Svep1 signalling pathways completely blocks the development of all facial lymphatic structures.
source: Only simultaneous interference of both the Vegfc and Svep1 signalling pathways completely blocked the development of all facial lymphatic structures (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Demonstrated by analysis of svep1;ccbe1 double mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: BLECs are absent in most svep1 mutants at 3 dpf, but some embryos show reduced or wildtype-like numbers.
source: In svep1 mutants, BLECs were found to be absent in most cases, but some embryos showed either reduced numbers or – in rare cases – even wildtype-like numbers of BLECs at 3 dpf (Figure 2A, B)
evidence: Quantified from confocal imaging of BLECs in svep1 mutants (Figure 2A, B).

claim: svep1 expressing cells are in close proximity to migrating BLECs at 3 dpf.
source: we observed svep1 expressing cells in close proximity to the migrating BLECs at 3 dpf (Figure 2C, D)
evidence: Shown by confocal imaging of svep1:Gal4; UAS:RFP transgenic embryos (Figure 2C, D).

claim: tie1 mutant embryos show the same facial lymphatic defects as svep1 mutant embryos at 3 dpf, with the FCLV being strongly affected.
source: Significantly, tie1 mutant embryos showed the same facial lymphatic defects as svep1 mutant embryos at 3 dpf (Figure 3A), with the FCLV being strongly affected
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal imaging comparing tie1 and svep1 mutants (Figure 3A).

claim: tie1 mutants do not show any BLECs at 3 dpf.
source: tie1 mutants did not show any BLECs at 3 dpf
evidence: Shown by confocal imaging and quantification (Figure 3B, D).

claim: tie1 mutants exhibit significantly reduced numbers of PLs at 2 dpf, similar to svep1 mutants.
source: tie1 mutants did not show any BLECs at 3 dpf and exhibited significantly reduced numbers of PLs at 2 dpf, similar to svep1 mutants (Figure 3B–E)
evidence: Quantified from confocal imaging (Figure 3C, E).

claim: tie2 mutant embryos display normal facial lymphatics, BLECs and PL numbers.
source: Importantly, tie2 mutant embryos, when examined for the same anatomical features, were found to display normal facial lymphatics, BLECs and PL numbers (Figure 3A–C and E)
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal imaging and quantification (Figure 3A-C, E).

claim: Around 40-50% of PLs in sibling embryos migrate along the artery from 2.5 to 3.5 dpf.
source: While around 40–50% of PLs in sibling embryos migrated along the artery, only 11% of PLs in tie1 and svep1 mutants showed migration in either dorsal or ventral direction along the artery (Figure 4M, N)
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse imaging (Figure 4M, N).

claim: Only 11% of PLs in tie1 and svep1 mutants show migration in either dorsal or ventral direction along the artery from 2.5 to 3.5 dpf.
source: While around 40–50% of PLs in sibling embryos migrated along the artery, only 11% of PLs in tie1 and svep1 mutants showed migration in either dorsal or ventral direction along the artery (Figure 4M, N)
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse imaging (Figure 4M, N).

claim: Around 33% of PLs in tie1 mutants undergo apoptosis from 2.5 to 3.5 dpf.
source: Additionally, we observed around 33% apoptotic PLs in tie1 mutants and 55% in svep1 mutants
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse imaging (Figure 4M, N).

claim: Around 55% of PLs in svep1 mutants undergo apoptosis from 2.5 to 3.5 dpf.
source: Additionally, we observed around 33% apoptotic PLs in tie1 mutants and 55% in svep1 mutants
evidence: Quantified from time-lapse imaging (Figure 4M, N).

claim: PLs in svep1 and tie1 mutants show significantly less migration in ventral and dorsal directions compared to siblings.
source: PLs in svep1 as well as in tie1 mutants showed significantly less migration in ventral and dorsal directions compared to siblings, while the mean velocity and total migration distance were unchanged
evidence: Quantified from cell tracking analysis (Figure 4P, R).

claim: The mean velocity and total migration distance of PLs are unchanged in svep1 and tie1 mutants compared to siblings.
source: PLs in svep1 as well as in tie1 mutants showed significantly less migration in ventral and dorsal directions compared to siblings, while the mean velocity and total migration distance were unchanged
evidence: Quantified from cell tracking analysis (Figure 4P, R).

claim: tie1 mutants treated with 0.014% tricaine from 30 to 48 hpf exhibit significantly more gaps in the DLAV at 2 dpf compared to untreated tie1 mutants.
source: Our analysis showed that tie1 mutants treated with tricaine exhibited significantly more gaps and fewer lumenized DLAV segments (Figure 5D) compared to both untreated tie1 mutants (Figure 5B) and treated siblings (Figure 5C, E, F)
evidence: Quantified from confocal imaging (Figure 5E, F).

claim: tie1 mutants treated with 0.014% tricaine from 30 to 48 hpf exhibit fewer lumenized DLAV segments at 2 dpf compared to untreated tie1 mutants.
source: Our analysis showed that tie1 mutants treated with tricaine exhibited significantly more gaps and fewer lumenized DLAV segments (Figure 5D) compared to both untreated tie1 mutants (Figure 5B) and treated siblings (Figure 5C, E, F)
evidence: Quantified from confocal imaging (Figure 5E, F).

claim: tie2 mutants do not show any defects in DLAV formation upon tricaine treatment.
source: For tie2 and vegfc mutants we did not observe any defects in DLAV formation upon tricaine treatment, indicating that this phenotype is specific for loss of Svep1 and Tie1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal imaging and quantification (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: vegfc mutants do not show any defects in DLAV formation upon tricaine treatment.
source: For tie2 and vegfc mutants we did not observe any defects in DLAV formation upon tricaine treatment, indicating that this phenotype is specific for loss of Svep1 and Tie1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal imaging and quantification (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: apelin expressing ECs are increased in ISVs of tie1 mutants upon tricaine treatment.
source: Additionally, upon tricaine treatment, and even in untreated conditions, apelin expressing ECs were increased in ISVs of tie1 mutants as already shown for svep1 morphants treated with tricaine in Coxam et al., 2022 (Figure 5G–J)
evidence: Quantified from confocal imaging (Figure 5L).

claim: apelin expressing ECs are increased in ISVs of tie1 mutants even in untreated conditions.
source: Additionally, upon tricaine treatment, and even in untreated conditions, apelin expressing ECs were increased in ISVs of tie1 mutants as already shown for svep1 morphants treated with tricaine in Coxam et al., 2022 (Figure 5G–J)
evidence: Quantified from confocal imaging (Figure 5L).

claim: svep1 morphants show increased apelin expression in the ISVs even without tricaine treatment.
source: svep1 morphants already showed increased apelin expression in the ISVs in untreated conditions ( Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal imaging and quantification (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: An additional loss of one or two functional copies of tie2 does not further affect PL numbers in tie1 mutant embryos at 2 dpf.
source: While tie1 mutants showed a highly significant reduction in PL numbers (Figure 6D, G), we found that an additional loss of one or two functional copies of tie2 did not further affect PL numbers in tie1 mutant embryos (Figure 6E–G)
evidence: Quantified from confocal imaging (Figure 6G).

claim: Loss of one tie1 allele in tie2 mutants does not result in any defects in PL numbers at 2 dpf.
source: Additionally, loss of one tie1 allele in tie2 mutants did not result in any defects (Figure 6C, G)
evidence: Quantified from confocal imaging (Figure 6G).

claim: Heterozygous loss of tie1 does not reveal any defects in TD formation in tie2 mutants at 5 dpf.
source: To further exclude contributions of Tie2 at later stages of lymphatic development on TD formation, we quantified the segments of TD across 10 consecutive trunk segments at 5 dpf. In line with our analysis at 2 dpf, heterozygous loss of tie1 did not reveal any defects in tie2 mutants (Figure 6H)
evidence: Quantified from confocal imaging (Figure 6H).

claim: svep1; tie1 double heterozygous embryos do not show any PL number reduction at 2 dpf compared to siblings.
source: In svep1; tie1 double heterozygous embryos we could not observe any PL number reduction, reduction of BLECs or reduced facial lymphatics compared to siblings (Figure 7A, B, H; Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Quantified from confocal imaging (Figure 7H).

claim: PL defects are significantly exacerbated in svep1+/−; tie1−/− compared to svep1+/+; tie1−/− mutant embryos at 2 dpf.
source: Importantly, these defects were significantly exacerbated in svep1+/−; tie1−/− compared to svep1+/+; tie1−/− mutant embryos (Figure 7D, F, H)
evidence: Quantified from confocal imaging showing genetic interaction (Figure 7H).

claim: Zebrafish Tie1 shows robust binding with zebrafish Svep1 in co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: Tie1 showed robust binding with Svep1 in every experiment (seven out of seven independent experiments; Figure 8A)
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 8A).

claim: Zebrafish Tie2 co-precipitated with zebrafish Svep1 in only two out of four experiments.
source: while Tie2 co-precipitated with Svep1 in only two out of four experiments (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Human TIE1 binds to the C-terminus of human SVEP1 (aa: 2261–3571).
source: We could observe that TIE1 showed binding to SVEP1, demonstrating that the SVEP1/TIE1 interaction is evolutionary conserved (Figure 8B)
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments using human proteins (Figure 8B).

claim: Purified human SVEP1 protein (C-terminus) binds to human TIE1 in pull-down assays.
source: After pull-down of SVEP1, we detected binding of SVEP1 with TIE1 (Figure 8C)
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assays using purified SVEP1 protein (Figure 8C).

claim: Purified human SVEP1 protein (C-terminus) shows no significant binding to human TIE2 in pull-down assays.
source: After pull-down of SVEP1, we detected binding of SVEP1 with TIE1 (Figure 8C) but no significant binding of TIE2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down assays using purified SVEP1 protein (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The lymphatic system provides essential functions for tissue fluid homeostasis, absorption of dietary fats, and immune surveillance.
source: The lymphatic system is part of the vasculature and provides essential functions for tissue fluid homeostasis, absorption of dietary fats, and immune surveillance
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about lymphatic system function.

claim: Malfunction of the lymphatic vasculature can lead to severe lymphedema, obesity, or chronic inflammatory diseases.
source: Malfunction of the lymphatic vasculature can lead to severe lymphedema, obesity, or chronic inflammatory diseases (Mäkinen et al., 2021; Oliver et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mice and zebrafish have served as popular model organisms to study the development of lymphatic vessels.
source: To that end, mice and zebrafish have served as popular model organisms to study the development of lymphatic vessels and are commonly used for analyzing the underlying genetic and molecular mechanisms (Mäkinen et al., 2007; Padberg et al., 2017; van Impel and Schulte-Merker, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Many genes essential for lymphangiogenesis in zebrafish are evolutionarily conserved and their inactivation leads to lymphatic defects in zebrafish and mice.
source: Furthermore, many genes that are essential for lymphangiogenesis in zebrafish are evolutionarily conserved. Their inactivation leads to lymphatic defects in zebrafish and mice, and mutations in their orthologues are causative for human diseases (Alders et al., 2009; Gordon et al., 2013; Hogan et al., 2009; Mauri et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Lympho-venous sprouts arise from the posterior cardinal vein at 32 hours post-fertilization in zebrafish trunk vasculature.
source: In the trunk vasculature of the zebrafish, so-called lympho-venous sprouts arise from the posterior cardinal vein at 32 hours post-fertilization (hpf)
evidence: Established knowledge about zebrafish lymphatic development.

claim: Parachordal lymphangioblasts (PLs) migrate along the horizontal myoseptum at 2 days post fertilization in zebrafish.
source: They migrate dorsally and either remodel an intersegmental artery into a vein, or they migrate along the so-called horizontal myoseptum (HM) as parachordal lymphangioblasts (PLs) at 2 days post fertilization (dpf)
evidence: Established knowledge about zebrafish lymphatic development.

claim: At 3 dpf, PLs migrate dorsally and ventrally to form the trunk lymphatic vasculature in zebrafish.
source: At 3 dpf, PLs migrate dorsally and ventrally to form the trunk lymphatic vasculature, consisting of the dorsal longitudinal lymphatic vessel, the intersegmental lymphatic vessels, and the thoracic duct (TD) (Hogan et al., 2009; Hogan and Schulte-Merker, 2017; Padberg et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The facial lymphatic network arises from three progenitor populations: PHS-LP, a migratory angioblast cell near the ventral aorta, and the major population sprouting from the CCV.
source: A separate lymphatic network, the facial lymphatics, arises in a distinctly different manner, originating from three progenitor populations: (1) the primary head sinus-lymphatic progenitors (PHS-LP), (2) a migratory angioblast cell near the ventral aorta, and (3) the major population sprouting from the common cardinal vein (CCV) (Eng et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Brain lymphatic endothelial cells (BLECs) are single endothelial cells residing within the leptomeningeal layer of the zebrafish brain.
source: A third lymphatic bed is composed of the brain lymphatic endothelial cells (BLECs), which are single endothelial cells residing within the leptomeningeal layer of the zebrafish brain and that arise from the choroidal vascular plexus (Bower et al., 2017; van Lessen et al., 2017; Galanternik et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: BLECs arise from the choroidal vascular plexus.
source: A third lymphatic bed is composed of the brain lymphatic endothelial cells (BLECs), which are single endothelial cells residing within the leptomeningeal layer of the zebrafish brain and that arise from the choroidal vascular plexus (Bower et al., 2017; van Lessen et al., 2017; Galanternik et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: VEGFC is secreted as a pro-form that is processed through the concerted activity of CCBE1 and Adamts3/14 in the extracellular space.
source: The best-studied pathway driving lymphangiogenesis comprises the growth factor Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor C (VEGFC), which is secreted as a pro-form that is processed through the concerted activity of Collagen and Calcium-Binding EGF domain-containing protein 1 (CCBE1) (Bos et al., 2011; Hogan et al., 2009; Jeltsch et al., 2014; Le Guen et al., 2014; Roukens et al., 2015) and a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with thrombospondin motifs (Adamts) 3/14 (Jeltsch et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2020) in the extracellular space
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Fully processed VEGFC binds to its receptor VEGFR3 as well as VEGFR2 and induces lymphangiogenesis.
source: Fully processed VEGFC binds to its receptor VEGFR3 as well as VEGFR2 and induces lymphangiogenesis (Joukov et al., 1997; Karkkainen et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TIE-ANG signalling is essential for lymphangiogenesis and vessel remodelling in mice and humans.
source: Apart from the VEGFC/VEGFR3 pathway, TIE-ANG signalling was shown to be essential for lymphangiogenesis and vessel remodelling in mice and humans
evidence: Established knowledge about TIE-ANG signalling.

claim: In mammals, TIE signalling is activated through binding of Angiopoietins to TIE2.
source: In mammals, TIE signalling is activated through binding of Angiopoietins to TIE2 (Davis et al., 1996; Maisonpierre et al., 1997)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: TIE1 can either block or activate the TIE signalling cascade in a context-dependent manner by forming heterodimers with TIE2.
source: TIE1 can either block or activate the signalling cascade in a context-dependent manner by forming heterodimers with TIE2 (Hansen et al., 2010; Marron et al., 2000; Saharinen et al., 2005; Savant et al., 2015; Seegar et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tie1 knockout mice display haemorrhages from E13.5 to P0, which lead to death and are preceded by lymphatic defects and edema formation from E12.5 onwards.
source: Tie1 knockout mice display haemorrhages from E13.5 to P0, which lead to death and are preceded by lymphatic defects and edema formation from E12.5 onwards (D'Amico et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Tie2 mutant mice die at E9.5–10.5 due to defective cardiac development and vascular remodelling.
source: In contrast to Tie1 mutant mice, Tie2 mutant mice die already at E9.5–10.5 due to defective cardiac development and vascular remodelling (Dumont et al., 1994; Sato et al., 1995)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Conditional knockout of Tie2 in lymphatic cells revealed the importance of TIE2 for lymphatic vessel development in mice especially for Schlemm's canal formation.
source: Conditional knockout of Tie2 in lymphatic cells revealed the importance of TIE2 for lymphatic vessel development in mice especially for Schlemm's canal formation (Kim et al., 2017; Thomson et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Conditional Tie1 deletion, Tie1;Tie2 double deletion and Ang2 blocking result in impaired postnatal lymphatic capillary network development in mice.
source: Recently, Korhonen et al. showed that conditional Tie1 deletion, Tie1;Tie2 double deletion and Ang2 blocking resulted in impaired postnatal lymphatic capillary network development in mice (Korhonen et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: tie2 mutant zebrafish do not have any overt vascular defects.
source: In zebrafish, tie2 mutants do not have any overt vascular defects (Gjini et al., 2011; Jiang et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: tie1 mutant zebrafish show cardiac morphogenesis and vascular defects including impaired brain angiogenesis, reduced CCV width, and impaired caudal vein plexus formation.
source: while tie1 mutants show cardiac morphogenesis and vascular defects (Carlantoni et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Svep1 encodes a large extracellular matrix molecule with a total of 3571 amino acids and a variety of protein domains.
source: Svep1 encodes a large extracellular matrix molecule, with a total of 3571 amino acids and a variety of protein domains
evidence: Established knowledge about Svep1 protein structure.

claim: Svep1−/− mice show normal development of the primitive lymphatic plexus until E12.5, but then fail to undergo remodelling of lymphatic vessels and formation of lymphatic valves at later embryonic stages.
source: Svep1−/− mice show normal development of the primitive lymphatic plexus until E12.5, but then fail to undergo remodelling of lymphatic vessels and formation of lymphatic valves at later embryonic stages, accompanied by edema formation and death postnatally (Karpanen et al., 2017; Morooka et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: SVEP1 has possible implications in lymphedema formation in human patients.
source: Recently, Michelini et al. reported possible implications of SVEP1 in lymphedema formation in human patients, underlining the importance of SVEP1 for the lymphatic vasculature (Michelini et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: SVEP1 is required for Schlemm's canal formation in mice.
source: Additionally, SVEP1 is also required for Schlemm's canal formation in mice (Thomson et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: svep1 mutant zebrafish exhibit a near-complete loss of the thoracic duct.
source: In zebrafish, svep1 mutants exhibit a near-complete loss of the TD, demonstrating an essential function during lymphangiogenesis in zebrafish (Karpanen et al., 2017; Morooka et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Murine SVEP1 binds to the α9 form of integrin (ITGA9) in vitro.
source: Murine SVEP1 has been shown to bind to the α9 form of integrin (ITGA9) as well as the TIE2 ligands ANG1 and ANG2 in vitro (Morooka et al., 2017; Sato-Nishiuchi et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Murine SVEP1 binds to the TIE2 ligands ANG1 and ANG2 in vitro.
source: Murine SVEP1 has been shown to bind to the α9 form of integrin (ITGA9) as well as the TIE2 ligands ANG1 and ANG2 in vitro (Morooka et al., 2017; Sato-Nishiuchi et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Compound heterozygous mutations for SVEP1 and TIE2 have been reported in human glaucoma patients.
source: Since compound heterozygous mutations for SVEP1 and TIE2 have recently been reported in human glaucoma patients, our data have clinical relevance in demonstrating a role for SVEP1 in TIE signalling in an in vivo setting
evidence: Supported by reference to clinical data.

claim: SVEP1 acts as a genetic modifier of TIE2-related primary congenital glaucoma (PCG).
source: Since recent clinical data suggested SVEP1 as a genetic modifier of TIE2-related primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) (Young et al., 2020), our results have clinical relevance and will further help to understand the molecular basis of PCG
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The FCLV forms independently of the Vegfc/Vegfr3 pathway but depends on Svep1.
source: Therefore, we identified a lymphatic structure in the zebrafish that, in contrast to all other lymphatic structures, forms independently of the Vegfc/Vegfr3 pathway, but depends on Svep1
evidence: Inferred from the complementary phenotypes of svep1 and vegfc pathway mutants.

claim: Svep1 and Tie1 interact genetically in vivo during early steps of lymphangiogenesis.
source: Our results provide the first in vivo evidence for svep1 and tie1 genetic interaction, thus placing Svep1 as an important regulator of Tie1 function
evidence: Demonstrated by genetic interaction studies showing exacerbated phenotypes in compound mutants.

claim: Svep1 is an important regulator of Tie1 function.
source: Our results provide the first in vivo evidence for svep1 and tie1 genetic interaction, thus placing Svep1 as an important regulator of Tie1 function
evidence: Inferred from genetic interaction data and protein binding assays.

claim: The SVEP1/TIE1 interaction is evolutionarily conserved between zebrafish and humans.
source: We could observe that TIE1 showed binding to SVEP1, demonstrating that the SVEP1/TIE1 interaction is evolutionary conserved (Figure 8B)
evidence: Demonstrated by binding assays showing interaction in both zebrafish and human proteins.

claim: Svep1/Tie1 signalling is important for lymphangiogenesis and acts, at least to some extent, in a Vegfc-independent manner.
source: Therefore, we conclude that svep1/tie1 signalling is not only important for lymphangiogenesis but also for blood vessel development and acts, at least to some extent, in a Vegfc-independent manner
evidence: Inferred from the observation that FCLV forms in vegfc mutants but not in svep1/tie1 mutants.

claim: Svep1/Tie1 signalling is important for blood vessel development.
source: Therefore, we conclude that svep1/tie1 signalling is not only important for lymphangiogenesis but also for blood vessel development and acts, at least to some extent, in a Vegfc-independent manner
evidence: Demonstrated by DLAV defects in tie1 mutants under reduced flow conditions.

claim: The FCLV is morphologically and functionally different from other lymphatic vessels.
source: Since the Schlemm's canal is a hybrid vessel (Kizhatil et al., 2014) and the FCLV seems to be also morphological and functional different from other lymphatic vessels (Shin et al., 2019), these two vessels not only share mechanistical but also functional differences to other lymphatic structures
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Inactivation of Angpt1 and Angpt2 or Tie2 completely abolishes Schlemm's canal development in mice.
source: Interestingly, inactivation of Angpt1 and Angpt2 or Tie2 completely abolishes Schlemm's canal development and leads to glaucoma formation in mice, while the Schlemm's canal is still present and only reduced in mice lacking Vegfc and Vegfd or Vegfr3, indicating that in some lymphatic structures VEGFC is not strictly required (Bernier-Latmani and Petrova, 2017; Thomson and Quaggin, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The Schlemm's canal is still present and only reduced in mice lacking Vegfc and Vegfd or Vegfr3.
source: Interestingly, inactivation of Angpt1 and Angpt2 or Tie2 completely abolishes Schlemm's canal development and leads to glaucoma formation in mice, while the Schlemm's canal is still present and only reduced in mice lacking Vegfc and Vegfd or Vegfr3, indicating that in some lymphatic structures VEGFC is not strictly required (Bernier-Latmani and Petrova, 2017; Thomson and Quaggin, 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Conditional knockout of Svep1 or Tie2 leads to high intraocular pressure and altered Schlemm's canal morphology in mice.
source: In mice, conditional knockout of Svep1 or Tie2 leads to high intraocular pressure and altered Schlemm's canal morphology (Li et al., 2020; Thomson et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tie2 and Tie1 expression levels are downregulated in Svep1 mutant mice.
source: Additionally, Tie2 and Tie1 expression levels are downregulated in Svep1 mutant mice (Morooka et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Teleost tie2 has been lost in the Acanthomorphata lineage, comprising 60% of contemporary teleost species.
source: Teleost tie2 has actually been lost in the Acanthomorphata lineage, comprising 60% of contemporary teleost species (Jiang et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: tie1 mutant zebrafish embryos display severe lymphatic defects in the head and trunk vasculature.
source: We here show that tie1 mutant zebrafish embryos display severe lymphatic defects in the head and trunk vasculature, in addition to the previously reported cardiac and blood vascular phenotypes including impaired brain angiogenesis, reduced CCV width, and impaired caudal vein plexus formation (Carlantoni et al., 2021)
evidence: Demonstrated by confocal imaging and quantification in this study.

claim: tie1 mutants develop strong edema at 4 dpf.
source: Since tie1 mutants developed strong edema at 4 dpf (data not shown), we focused our analysis on lymphatic phenotypes at 2 and 3 dpf to exclude secondary effects on the lymphatic vasculature
evidence: Observed during the study.

claim: Treatment of embryos with 0.014% tricaine between 30 and 48 hpf leads to incomplete formation of the DLAV with gaps and non-lumenized DLAV segments at 2 dpf in svep1 mutant embryos.
source: Treatment of embryos with 0.014% tricaine between 30 and 48 hpf leads to incomplete formation of the dorsal longitudinal anastomotic vessel (DLAV) with gaps and non-lumenized DLAV segments at 2 dpf in svep1 mutant embryos. This phenotype is accompanied by increased Vegfa/Vegfr signalling and increased number of Apelin positive tip cells (Coxam et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The specific absence of the FCLV is unique to svep1 and tie1 mutants and not observed in other lymphatic mutants.
source: while reduced PL numbers and TD length is a hallmark feature of many lymphatic mutants, the specific absence of the FCLV is unique, and common to both mutants
evidence: Inferred from comparison of multiple mutant phenotypes.

claim: Svep1 could act as a direct ligand for Tie1.
source: Second, and due to the close proximity of svep1 expressing cells to LECs, Svep1 could also act as a direct ligand for Tie1
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on expression patterns and binding data.

claim: Svep1 could be an essential component of enabling or stabilizing binding of angiopoietins to Tie1.
source: First, and based on the observation that murine Svep1 can bind Tie receptor ligands (Morooka et al., 2017), zebrafish Svep1 could be an essential component of enabling or stabilizing binding of angiopoietins to Tie1
evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on published data about murine Svep1.

claim: The C-terminus of Svep1 is critical for Svep1 function.
source: For human SVEP1 we only used the C-terminus for binding assays, since we reasoned, based on a previously generated svep1 mutant line (Ly05-265) with a premature stop in CCP domain 9 (Karpanen et al., 2017), that the C-terminus is critical for Svep1 function
evidence: Inferred from the phenotype of a mutant line with a premature stop codon.

claim: Zebrafish can serve as an in vivo model for clinically relevant aspects of Svep1/Tie signalling.
source: Together with the recent discovery that SVEP1 could act as a modifier of TEK-related PCG disease penetrance, further studies in zebrafish can serve as an in vivo model for clinically relevant aspects of Svep1/Tie signalling
evidence: Inferred from the conservation of SVEP1/TIE1 interaction and clinical relevance.

claim: tie1 expression levels are not downregulated in zebrafish svep1 mutants.
source: However, using in situ hybridization, we did not find any signs of miss-regulation of tie1 expression in svep1 mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), indicating that at least in zebrafish downregulation of tie1 is not causative for the observed defects
evidence: Demonstrated by in situ hybridization (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).

claim: The severity of facial lymphatic defects varies between individual svep1 mutant embryos.
source: Although the formation of the FCLV was strongly affected in all svep1 mutants analyzed, the severity of the defects of facial lymphatic structures varied between individual svep1 mutant embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Observed from imaging multiple svep1 mutant embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Apoptotic events in PLs could be a consequence of failed migration or decreased survival due to absent Svep1 or Tie1 activity.
source: These apoptotic events could be a consequence of failed migration, or could be due to decreased survival as a direct consequence of absent Svep1 or Tie1 activity
evidence: Speculative interpretation of observed apoptosis data.

claim: Svep1 and Tie1 are required for PL migration along the arteries in dorsal or ventral direction.
source: Therefore, we can conclude that Svep1 and Tie1 are required for PL migration along the arteries in dorsal or ventral direction
evidence: Inferred from cell tracking data showing reduced dorsal/ventral migration.

claim: TIE1 is a ligand for SVEP1.
source: Therefore, we conclude that TIE1 is a ligand for SVEP1
evidence: Concluded from pull-down and co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Tie signalling is not only required in mice and humans for lymphatic vessel formation, but also in zebrafish.
source: However, we here show definitively that Tie signalling is not only required in mice and humans for lymphatic vessel formation, but also in zebrafish
evidence: Demonstrated by lymphatic phenotypes in tie1 mutant zebrafish.

claim: There is close juxtaposition of svep1 expressing cells with migrating LECs in all developing lymphatic structures examined.
source: Thus, there is close juxtaposition of svep1 expressing cells with migrating LECs in all developing lymphatic structures examined, including the PLs in the trunk (Karpanen et al., 2017)
evidence: Observed from expression pattern analysis in this study and cited literature.

claim: Tie1 signalling has an important function during lymphangiogenesis in zebrafish.
source: Therefore, our study demonstrates an important function for Tie1 signalling during lymphangiogenesis as well as blood vessel development in zebrafish
evidence: Demonstrated by lymphatic phenotypes in tie1 mutants.

claim: Tie1 signalling has an important function during blood vessel development in zebrafish.
source: Therefore, our study demonstrates an important function for Tie1 signalling during lymphangiogenesis as well as blood vessel development in zebrafish
evidence: Demonstrated by DLAV defects in tie1 mutants under reduced flow.

claim: The FCLV and facial lymphatics have functional and morphological differences.
source: Until recently, it was traditionally considered, that lymphatic vessels always (1) have a venous origin and (2) need Vegfc signalling to develop. In the last decade, it was shown that lymphatic vessels can also have non-venous origins in mice (Martinez-Corral et al., 2015) and also in the facial lymphatics of zebrafish (Eng et al., 2019). However, Vegfc signalling seemed to be always required for lymphatic vessel development
evidence: Supported by citations and the differential requirements for Vegfc vs Svep1/Tie1.

claim: A specific progenitor population of zebrafish facial lymphatic network, forming the FCLV, develops in a Vegfc-independent, but Svep1/Tie1-dependent mechanism.
source: Here, we make the significant finding that a specific progenitor population of zebrafish facial lymphatic network, forming the FCLV, develops in a Vegfc-independent, but Svep1/Tie1-dependent mechanism
evidence: Demonstrated by the complementary phenotypes of vegfc and svep1/tie1 mutants.
